A kidney machine built from sausage skins. In 1943, in occupied Netherlands, kidney failure meant death within days.

Willem Kolff, 32, a doctor in Kampen, had no way to clean a patient's blood. So he wound cellophane tubing, made from sausage casing, around a rotating drum that turned in a tank of fluid. Blood ran through the tubing, waste passed out into the fluid, clean blood returned to the patient.

14 of his first 15 patients died. In September 1945, patient 17, a 67-year-old woman in a coma, woke after hours on the machine. She lived 7 more years. Today about 1.5 million people are on dialysis, and every treatment is still built on his idea.

Builders wanted. The Ad Astra Fellowship: 12 months, a room, food, the labs, the machine shop and the compute at $0, a company in your name from day 1. 1 written application, no credentials needed. Apply at joinadastra.com

Sources: Lasker Foundation (Kolff's own account, 2002, and the hemodialysis award page), National WWII Museum, Kidney Care UK.
